fetched_contents.text: Effect of Temperature on Material Properties of Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) Tendons: Experiments and Model Assessment Abstract Material properties at elevated temperatures are important factors in the fire safety design and numerical analysis of concrete members strengthened with fiber reinforced polymer (FRP) composites. Most of the previous research mainly focused on tensile strength and elastic modulus in conventional steady state temperature tests. However, the transient state test method is more realistic for strengthening concrete structures. At the same time, the coefficient of thermal expansion of FRP composites is also one of the important factors affecting concrete members at elevated temperatures. This paper presents a detailed experimental investigation on the longitudinal thermal expansion deformation, and the mechanical properties of carbon FRP (CFRP) tendons with 8 mm diameter in the steady state and transient state. The results indicate that longitudinal deformation of CFRP tendons is negative at high temperature; in addition, the transient state test results of CFRP tendons are slightly higher than the steady state test results. The final part of this paper assesses the accuracy of different empirical models. Furthermore, a new equation calculating the properties of CFRP composites at elevated temperatures is presented with the numerical fitting technique, which is in good agreement with the experimental results. Keywords: carbon fiber reinforced polymer, material properties, experimental tests, elevated temperatures, modeling 1. Introduction In recent years, the application of fiber reinforced polymer (FRP) composites has increased significantly in civil engineering structures around the world. It is mainly attributed to the fact that FRP composites have many advantages compared with steel, such as high strength-to-weight ratio, corrosion resistance, fatigue resistance, and non-magnetic properties. Although numerous investigations have shown that FRP composites are effective materials for concrete members [1,2], many challenges still exist in the increasing application of FRP composites. One of these challenges is to fully understand the material properties of FRP composites at elevated temperatures. Due to the fact that FRP composites are typically produced from the thermosetting polymer matrix, their mechanical properties deteriorate severely when exposed to fire. Even though FRP composites embedded in the concrete do not burn due to lack of oxygen, the resin will soften and decompose when the temperature exceeds the glass transition temperature (Tg) and the decomposition temperature (Td). The softening and decomposition of the resin not only reduces the strength of the resin itself, but also weakens the bonding effect of fibers, resulting in the rapid reduction of the strength of FRP composites. The research conducted by Yu Bai [3,4], has indicated that the mechanical properties of FRP composites are affected significantly by their thermal properties when subjected to elevated and high temperatures. Furthermore, the thermo–mechanical behavior of FRP composites depends mainly on the states (glassy, leathery, rubbery, and decomposed) of the polymer resin at high temperature. In the experimental study of glass FRP (GFRP) composites, it was also confirmed that the elastic modulus and strength decreased significantly at raised temperatures, which reached the range of glass transition and decomposition temperatures [5]. Similarly, Yu Baolin [6] tested two types of near surface mounted (NSM) carbon FRP (CFRP) composites. It was found that the strength of both CFRP strip and rod dropped dramatically when the temperature reached and exceeded Tg (around 80 °C) and Td (around 300 °C). Since the low Tg of resin is the greater shortcoming of FRP composites at elevated temperatures, an improved resin with a higher Tg was tested by Zhu [7]. After improving the Tg of basalt FRP (BFRP) composites, the concrete beams strengthened with near surface mounted (NSM) BFRP bars exhibited better fire resistance. Therefore, the comprehensive study of the high temperature characteristics of FRP composites can greatly improve the fire resistance of concrete members strengthened with FRP composites. In order to further understand the inherent properties of FRP composites at high temperature, Saafi M [8] suggested constitutive models for the mechanical properties of aramid FRP (AFRP) rebars, CFRP rebars, and glass FRP (GFRP) rebars linearly decreasing with temperature according to the experimental results of Blontrok [9]. However, a large amount of experimental research has shown that the tensile strength and elasticity modulus of FRP composites do not deteriorate linearly with temperature [10,11,12]. Therefore, Bisby [13] proposed a hyperbolic tangent function model based on the experimental data of relevant literature. The fitting coefficients were obtained by least square regression analysis. In order to fully reveal the influence of thermo–physical responses on thermo–mechanical properties, Gibson [14] successfully applied the glass transition temperature (Tg) and remaining resin content (RRC) criteria to the hyperbolic tangent function model. Subsequently, the Gibson’s model was modified by Yu [6] and Chowdhury [11], respectively. It is considered that Tg in Gibson’s model can be the critical temperature or the temperature around which the curve is nearly symmetrical rather than the glass transition temperature. Yu [6] carried out experimental testing of CFRP bars and CFRP slabs, and fitted the obtained results with the hyperbolic tangent function model. Nevertheless, with the improvement of the measurement methods, the curve of the mechanical properties was more and more similar to that of thermo–physical state of FRP composites at high temperatures [15,16]. Introduction The rapid deployment of hydrogen fuel cell vehicles (HFCVs) has received attention on the safety of on-board hydrogen storage systems, a challenge that remains central to their widespread adoption [[1], [2], [3], [4], [5]]. Type Ⅲ (metal liner reinforced with fully-wrapped composite material) and type Ⅳ (non-metallic liner reinforced with fully-wrapped composite material) cylinders are currently the preferred choice for compressed gaseous hydrogen (CGH2) storage because of their lightweight and high-strength properties [6,7]. These cylinders typically employ carbon fiber reinforced epoxy composites (CFRCs) as the overwrapping material, which plays a critical role in achieving the required mechanical performance and weight reduction. CFRCs are widely utilized in aerospace, automotive, and energy storage applications due to their high specific strength, high modulus, and excellent corrosion resistance [8,9]. When compared to alternatives like glass or basalt fiber composites, CFRCs provide offer superior mechanical performance and the most significant weight-saving potential. However, their thermal and fire resistance can be constrained by the polymeric matrix. Consequently, understanding their behavior under extreme heat is critical. When subjected to accidental fire exposure, the cylinders face severe risks: the thermosetting epoxy resin used in the composite gradually decomposes, mass loss accelerates [10], and the mechanical properties of the composites, such as strength, tend to degrade under heat radiation or fire impingement [[11], [12], [13]]. Understanding the thermal degradation and tensile behavior of carbon fiber composites under elevated temperatures is therefore essential for assessing the fire resistance and structural integrity of CGH2 cylinders. Fire-induced failure behaviors of CGH2 cylinders have often been analyzed with reference to previous studies on compressed natural gas (CNG) vessels, while accounting for the higher combustibility and explosivity of hydrogen. To address these fire safety challenges, various analytical and numerical models have been developed to predict cylinder burst capability and clarify the underlying damage mechanism [[14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]]. Among these, Damien Halm et al. [18]proposed global burst criteria grounded in the ply-level failure, requiring accurate temperature-dependent elastic moduli and strength parameters of unidirectional composite laminates as essential material inputs. While the probability model for the tensile strength of unidirectional carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) at room temperature have been established [20], predictive models incorporating high temperature degradation effects remain limited. Kashkarov et al. [21] reported a failure mechanism through decomposition temperatures ranging within the control volume of the carbon fiber reinforced polymer solid body. While Valencia et al. [19] emphasized that the bursting behavior was affected by the mechanical degradation at specific thermal stages. Taken together, these investigations highlight that predicting the fire resistance time of composite cylinders relies heavily on two aspects: a precise description of the temperature dependent thermal-mechanical properties of the composite material and the establishment of a reliable failure criterion. Previous experimental studies have consistently demonstrated that the tensile properties of CFRC exposed to fire or high temperatures are strongly influenced by material composition, thermal environment, and ply orientation [22,23]. In general, elevated temperatures cause a pronounced decline in tensile strengths of CFRP laminates, regardless of laminate geometry or size effects [24]. Sun et al. [25]reported that the tensile strength of CFRP laminates decreases nonlinearly with increasing temperature within a range of −30 °C–160 °C. Their experimental data were effectively modelled using a tanℎ function, correlating well with the experimental data. The effect of ply orientation further governs the thermomechanical response of CFRP laminates. Laminate with 0° middle plies exhibits faster temperature rises on both internal and rear surfaces compared to those with 45° middle plies, and the ply stacking pattern significantly affects the rate of quasi-isotropic laminate's tensile softening and the onset of failure under low applied tensile stresses (less than 50 % of the ultimate strength) [26]. Similarly, Hawileh [27] observed a 42 % reduction in tensile strength for composite carbon sheets conditioned at 250 °C (45-min exposure followed by 24-h cooling) compared to values at room temperature, attributed to partial epoxy loss and eventual sheet splitting. Beyond static heating, several researchers have explored coupled thermo-mechanical loading, revealing that thermal effects predominantly govern composite degradation, while additional bending loads contribute minimally to rear surface heating [28]. Nguyen et al. [29]further demonstrated that the in-situ thermo-mechanical strength of P-CFRP is significantly lower than the residual strength measured after mere thermal exposure (20 °C–700 °C), indicating that real-time thermal–mechanical coupling aggravates damage evolution. fetched_contents.text: Temperature-dependent mechanical properties and material modifications of carbon fiber composites for optimized structures in high-end industrial applications Introduction Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites have emerged as crucial materials in aerospace, automotive, and marine industries due to their exceptional strength-to-weight ratio, corrosion resistance, and design flexibility [[1], [2], [3]]. Among these, thermoset and thermoplastic composites are widely used due to their low viscosity, strong interfacial bonding with fibers, and superior mechanical properties [4,5]. As a result, carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites have gained significant attention due to their enhanced impact resistance, ease of processing, and recyclability [[6], [7], [8]]. CFRP composites, known for their high mechanical performance, are extensively utilized in load-bearing structures [8,9]. However, their behavior under varying environmental conditions, particularly temperature fluctuations and mechanical stresses, remains a critical concern [10]. Studies have shown that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing the modulus and strength, whereas lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [11,12]. The combined effects of temperature and mechanical factors such as pre-loading, bending, and impact loading require further investigation to ensure reliable performance in demanding applications. This review examines the impact of temperature and mechanical factors on composite behavior, analyzing their influence on mechanical properties and failure mechanisms. The assessment includes tensile, flexural, and interlaminar shear strength variations in CFRP composites subjected to different temperature conditions. To enhance the performance and durability of CFRP composites, researchers have explored various material modification techniques [13]. Interlayer toughening strategies, including the incorporation of thermoplastic films, nanoparticles, and interleaved structures, have been developed to mitigate issues like delamination and poor interlaminar strength [[14], [15], [16], [17]]. Halloysite nanotubes (HNTs), for instance, have demonstrated potential in improving adhesion and mechanical integrity in CFRP composites, particularly in extreme environmental conditions [18]. By modifying the adhesive and resin properties with HNTs, enhancements in mode-I and mode-II interlaminar fracture toughness (ILFT) have been observed, improving resistance to crack propagation and structural failure [18,19]. This review discusses recent advancements in material modification techniques aimed at enhancing fracture toughness, adhesive bonding, and overall composite performance, along with the trade-offs associated with these enhancements. In addition to material enhancements, the structural performance of composites is highly dependent on geometric factors, particularly in mechanically fastened joints [[20], [21], [22], [23]]. Open-hole, pinned-joint, and bolted-joint configurations are widely employed in composite structures but pose challenges due to stress concentrations that can significantly reduce mechanical strength [[24], [25], [26]]. While thermoplastic CFRP composites exhibit better damage tolerance their performance in joint structures [27,28], especially under temperature variations, requires further exploration. Studies indicate that geometric parameters such as width-to-hole diameter (W/D) and edge distance-to-hole diameter (E/D) ratios significantly influence the failure mechanisms, including shear-out, net tension, and bearing failures. This review evaluates the effects of geometry and temperature on the tensile properties of CFRP composites with different joint configurations and load distribution strategies. Advanced structural optimization techniques have further contributed to enhancing the mechanical behavior of CFRP composites [[29], [30], [31], [32]]. Filament winding processes, multi-material integration, and the incorporation of nanoparticles into interleaved structures have been explored to improve damage resistance, moisture stability, and impact performance [33,34]. The use of HNTs as an interleaved reinforcement method has shown promising results in enhancing moisture resistance, mechanical strength, and fracture toughness, particularly in CFRP composites subjected to humid [18] and cryogenic conditions. Research on optimizing fiber layups and hybrid fiber configurations has also been conducted to improve overall load distribution and stiffness retention [35]. Additionally, CFRP pipes designed for aerospace and naval applications must withstand varying environmental conditions, requiring innovative solutions for damage mitigation and long-term reliability [36,37]. This review highlights recent studies on optimizing CFRP structures, particularly through the use of HNTs for interleaved reinforcement and the enhancement of CFRP pipes for use in extreme environmental conditions. Given the increasing demand for high-performance, lightweight, and environmentally sustainable materials [38,39], understanding the interplay between temperature, mechanical factors, material modifications, and structural optimization techniques is essential. The development of functionally graded CFRP structures with tailored mechanical and thermal properties is a promising avenue for future applications. This review provides a critical analysis of recent technological developments in CFRP composites, offering insights into their behavior under diverse environmental conditions and their potential for future applications in high-performance industries such as aerospace, automotive, and marine engineering. The findings of this review contribute to the ongoing efforts to enhance composite material design, ensuring durability, sustainability, and superior mechanical performance in next-generation engineering applications. fetched_contents.text: Experimental and Numerical Studies on Temperature Dependent Failure Mechanisms of PW-CFRP Introduction Continuous carbon fiber reinforced polymer (C-CFRP) composites are extensively used in aerospace, automotive, rail transport, sports, and architecture due to their exceptional properties such as low weight, high specific strength, high specific stiffness, and excellent fatigue resistance [1,2]. In C-CFRP composites, continuous fibers serve as the reinforcing phase embedded within thermoplastic [3,4] or thermosetting [5,6] matrix materials. Most of matrix materials are highly temperature-sensitive. Notably, cryogenic temperatures cause the prevalence of potential cracks [7], and near the glass transition temperature, the strength and modulus drop sharply, posing significant challenges for CFRP applications across a wide range of temperatures [[7], [8], [9], [10]]. For unidirectional continuous fiber-reinforced composites, tensile strength and modulus along fiber direction 0° generally show a slight decrease as temperature rises from room temperature up to the glass transition temperature. Yu and Kodur [11] found that unidirectional CFRP with a glass transition temperature of 80°C exhibited a reduction of tensile strength and modulus as temperatures increased from 20°C to 600°C, retaining over 85% of their initial values at 100°C. Finazzi et al. [12] observed similar trends for unidirectional thermoplastic CFRP. Tensile strength and modulus in the 90° direction also tend to decrease with increasing temperature. Unlike the fiber, the matrix loses almost all load-bearing capacity near or above the glass transition temperature. This rapid decline is attributed to the pronounced softening effect of temperature on the matrix, which in turn affects the tensile properties in the 90° direction [10]. For environments ranging from cryogenic temperature to room temperature, findings are more variable. Li et al. [13] noted that the tensile modulus in both the 0° and 90° directions increased at low temperatures as compared to room temperature, a trend was also observed by Hamori et al. [14]. While Meng et al. [15] found that 0° tensile modulus decreased at low temperatures. Li et al. [13] reported a slight decrease of tensile strength at low temperatures, while Jia et al. [16] and Meng et al. [15] reported an increase of flexure strength at low temperature. This diversity may be attributed to the complex stress state in flexural test, which combines tensile, compressive, and shear stresses [17,18]. Given that the asymmetry in the tensile and compressive behavior of CFRP [19], different phenomena may be observed. These observations suggest that the temperature-dependent mechanical response under multiaxial stress states may fundamentally differ from that under uniaxial stress, highlighting a critical area for future investigation. Compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear properties are significantly influenced by the matrix, making them more sensitive to temperature than the fiber [20]. Compressive, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach the glass transition temperature [10,17]. At low temperatures, the matrix bonds well with the fibers, ensuring good load transfer [15], leading to increasing the resistance to failure with brittle fiber fracture, transverse matrix cracking, and delamination failure modes [9,16]. As temperature rises, matrix softening reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [16,18]. These findings collectively demonstrate that the macroscopic temperature-dependent mechanical properties of CFRPs are intrinsically linked to their underlying microscopic mechanisms and exhibit pronounced temperature-dependent tension-compression asymmetry. Unlike unidirectional composites, plain-woven (PW) CFRP demonstrates robust mechanical properties under multiaxial stress states due to its interwoven meso-scale structure, which reinforces fibers in two directions [21], resulting in fewer cracks and stronger interlaminar properties under thermal stress [7]. Similar to unidirectional composites, temperature significantly impacts tensile and shear properties related to the matrix [[22], [23], [24]]. Lu et al. [24] conducted axial tensile and compressive tests on plain-woven CFRP at temperatures ranging from 20°C to 150°C. As the temperature increased, a more pronounced reduction was observed in compressive strength compared to tensile strength, while the modulus showed no significant change. The macro and meso scale failure modes were also temperature-dependent. Nam et al. [25] performed axial compression tests on plain-woven carbon fabric reinforced polyamide (CF/PA) composites from room temperature (25°C) to 120°C. The results showed brittle shear failure at room temperature and 40°C, while at 60°C to 120°C, failure modes resembled kink band formation. Various woven fiber-reinforced composites exhibited consistent trends [[26], [27], [28], [29]]. A classical continuum damage mechanics (CDM) framework typically comprises four constitutive components: an elasticity model, plasticity model, damage initiation criterion and damage evolution law. Although woven composites have numerous advantages over unidirectional materials, the complex multiscale architecture of woven composites introduces more challenges in understanding and modeling their temperature-dependent behavior [30]. For instance, off-axis loading, which involves a combination of shear and tensile stresses, can induce yarn rotation in the loading direction, resulting in notable deformation and necking [31]. Below-Tg behavior: how strength and modulus evolve with temperature

Below the glass transition temperature (Tg), the mechanical behavior of CFRP is shaped by the stiffness of the fiber and matrix, the interfacial bonding, and the thermal softening of the matrix as temperature approaches Tg from below. The evidence suggests that the matrix is the main contributor to stiffness loss near Tg, because matrix softening reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. Below Tg, the matrix is still in a glassy state and generally stiffer, so the overall stiffness of the composite is supported by both fiber and matrix contributions. However, as temperature increases, the matrix becomes less rigid and less able to carry load, which weakens the composite’s stiffness relative to the fiber-dominated regime [N4-F4].

Regarding strength, the evidence indicates that strength can decrease with increasing temperature even below Tg. A study on CFRP plates exposed to elevated temperatures found that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3]. Another study on CFRP tendons reported that strength dropped dramatically when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C, although this is near- or above-Tg rather than strictly below-Tg [N2-R2]. The review evidence also states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, whereas lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This implies that, below Tg, the strength may decrease gradually with temperature, though the exact rate depends on matrix softening and interfacial behavior.

The role of matrix plasticization and fiber-matrix interaction is central. The evidence explicitly notes that matrix softening near or above Tg reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. It also emphasizes that compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach Tg, which is consistent with the idea that fiber-matrix interaction is weakened as matrix plasticization occurs [N4-F4]. Fiber breakage, on the other hand, is described as significantly influencing the loss of stiffness in the laminate, but not its strength [N4-R1]. This suggests that below Tg, stiffness loss is more strongly tied to matrix and interfacial degradation than to fiber fracture, while strength may decline more slowly or less visibly.

Overall, below Tg, modulus and strength both tend to decrease as temperature rises, but the evidence is not uniform enough to conclude a single monotonic rule. Some studies suggest a gradual decrease in strength and modulus with increasing temperature [N2-R3], while others indicate that modulus may be relatively stable or only slowly affected below Tg [N3-R4]. The clearest pattern is that matrix softening and fiber-matrix interaction govern the temperature-dependent response, with strength more sensitive to interfacial degradation than to fiber failure [N4-R1][N4-F4].

Above-Tg behavior: how strength and modulus change with increasing temperature

Above Tg, the mechanical response of CFRP becomes dominated by matrix softening, viscoelasticity, and long-term damage accumulation. The evidence is consistent that modulus decreases with increasing temperature above Tg, and in some cases, the decrease is dramatic. A review explicitly states that elevated temperatures reduce modulus and strength, while lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. Another study on CFRP plates found that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3], but this is not strong evidence for above-Tg behavior alone. A broader review on temperature-dependent CFRP mechanical properties states that studies have shown CFRP composites to decrease in tensile properties with increasing temperature, with the tensile properties mainly dependent on factors such as temperature and mechanical factors [N3-R2]. This supports the general conclusion that modulus and strength decline above Tg.

The strength response above Tg is more complex. Some studies report a significant drop in tensile strength with increasing temperature, including a 68% reduction in tensile strength after high-temperature exposure [N3-R5]. Another study found that CFRP tendons showed a dramatic drop in strength when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C [N2-R2]. The review evidence also notes that tensile properties decrease with increasing temperature and that the transition from brittle to ductile behavior occurs above Tg, with modulus and strength dropping [N3-F3]. These findings indicate that strength decreases above Tg, but the exact rate and magnitude depend on temperature, exposure time, and matrix degradation.

A key mechanism above Tg is matrix softening, which weakens the composite and increases damage accumulation. The evidence states that matrix softening near or above Tg reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. It also notes that compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach Tg, which is consistent with a broader temperature-dependent degradation trend [N4-F4]. Above Tg, this softening becomes more pronounced, and the matrix is no longer able to support as much load, so strength declines more sharply.

Viscoelasticity and long-term creep/damage accumulation are important above Tg. The review explicitly states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, while lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This implies that above Tg, the material behaves more viscoelastically, and the response is not purely elastic. The review also emphasizes that geometric parameters and joint configurations can significantly influence failure mechanisms and mechanical behavior, suggesting that above-Tg damage is not only a matter of material properties but also of stress concentrations and long-term loading history [N3-F3]. The evidence does not provide a detailed viscoelastic model for CFRP in this wave, but it does support the interpretation that long-term exposure above Tg leads to cumulative damage and a progressive loss of strength.

In summary, above Tg, modulus decreases with increasing temperature, and strength generally decreases as well, often more sharply. The main drivers are matrix softening, fiber-matrix interaction loss, and long-term damage accumulation. The evidence is strongest for a decrease in strength and modulus above Tg, with some studies showing dramatic reductions [N2-R2][N3-R5], but it is also clear that the exact temperature dependence can vary depending on exposure conditions and material composition [N3-F3].

Near-Tg behavior: transition effects on strength and modulus

Near Tg, the transition effects on strength and modulus are marked by a sharp or mixed response, depending on the direction of approach and the measurement protocol. The evidence indicates that the transition is not a simple continuous or abrupt change; rather, it is influenced by the temperature history, dwell time, and the state of the polymer matrix. A study on CFRP plates exposed to elevated temperatures reported that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3]. However, another study found that the strength of both CFRP strip and rod dropped dramatically when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C [N2-R2]. This implies that near Tg, the transition can be abrupt in some cases, especially when the temperature passes Tg, while the modulus may remain relatively stable or change only slightly.

The evidence also suggests that the transition is mixed in terms of the underlying mechanism. The review states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, whereas lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that near Tg, the material is transitioning between different failure modes, with stiffness and strength changing in response to matrix softening. The evidence from the experimental and numerical study of PW-CFRP further clarifies that, for unidirectional continuous fiber-reinforced composites, tensile strength and modulus along fiber direction 0° generally show a slight decrease as temperature rises from room temperature up to Tg, while the matrix loses almost all load-bearing capacity near or above Tg [N5-F4]. This means that near Tg, the composite’s behavior is governed by the matrix approaching its glass transition state, with the fiber still supporting some load but the matrix becoming increasingly soft.

The transition is also strongly affected by temperature rate and dwell time. The evidence notes that compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach Tg, and that the rate of quasi-isotropic laminate’s tensile softening and onset of failure under low applied tensile stresses is influenced by the ply stacking pattern [N4-F4]. Another study on CFRP plates under elevated temperatures found that the tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while the elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3], which suggests that dwell time and temperature history can smooth the apparent transition. The review also states that mechanical properties do not deteriorate linearly with temperature, and that experimental results do not always align with linear extrapolation [N3-F3]. This implies that the transition near Tg can appear continuous in some studies and more abrupt in others, depending on the measurement protocol.

In conclusion, near Tg the transition effects on strength and modulus are mixed: modulus may remain relatively stable or change only slightly, while strength often decreases sharply as temperature crosses Tg [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The transition is not cleanly continuous or abrupt; it is influenced by matrix softening, fiber-matrix interaction, temperature history, and dwell time [N4-F4][N5-F4]. The evidence supports the interpretation that near Tg the material moves from a stiffer, more brittle state to a softer, more ductile state, with strength declining more prominently than modulus in some cases [N3-F3][N5-F4].

Data sources, models, and experimental methods for temperature-dependent CFRP

The data sources and experimental methods used to study temperature-dependent CFRP are diverse, with a strong emphasis on steady-state, transient-state, and cyclic thermal exposure. One study reports a detailed experimental investigation on longitudinal thermal expansion deformation of CFRP tendons, including steady-state and transient-state tests [N1-F1]. Another study on CFRP plates exposed to elevated temperatures tested 30 CFRP specimens under elevated temperatures (10, 30, 50, 70, and 90°C) to explore degradations in tensile properties [N6-R4]. A study on thermal effects on additive manufactured CFRP composites at stable and cyclic temperature also indicates that temperature strongly influences matrix joining and material strength reduction [N6-R3]. These protocols suggest that common experimental approaches include controlled temperature exposure, tensile testing, and mechanical property assessment under varying thermal conditions.

The standards or protocols used are not explicitly listed in the evidence, but the experimental methods imply a reliance on standard tensile and mechanical testing procedures. The review on temperature-dependent mechanical properties and material modifications notes that the behavior of CFRP composites is influenced by temperature and mechanical factors, and that studies have focused on tensile, flexural, and interlaminar shear strength variations [N3-F3]. This indicates that the field uses conventional mechanical testing standards, though the exact standards are not named in the provided evidence. The evidence also mentions that some studies compare steady-state and transient-state test results, suggesting that temperature history and loading conditions are important experimental considerations [N1-F1][N6-R3].

Key analytical models and empirical fits used to describe temperature dependence include empirical fits, hyperbolic tangent functions, and multi-scale damage models. The evidence states that tensile strength and elasticity modulus do not deteriorate linearly with temperature, and that models such as the hyperbolic tangent function have been used [N3-F3]. It also notes that Saafi M suggested constitutive models for CFRP rebars, CFRP rebars, and GFRP rebars linearly decreasing with temperature according to experimental results [N1-F1], while Bisby proposed a hyperbolic tangent function model based on experimental data [N1-F1]. Gibson later applied Tg and remaining resin content criteria to the hyperbolic tangent model, and Yu and Chowdhury modified it [N1-F1]. These models are empirical fits designed to capture the non-linear temperature dependence of CFRP properties, especially near and above Tg.

The limitations of the data and how they affect interpretation are significant. The evidence repeatedly notes that the temperature dependence is non-linear and that experimental results do not always align with simple linear extrapolation [N3-F3][N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that the degradation behavior depends on material composition, thermal environment, ply orientation, and exposure conditions [N2-F2]. In addition, the review points out that most existing research has focused on residual properties after thermal exposure, offering limited insight into real-time degradation and failure evolution under simultaneous thermal and mechanical loading [N2-F2]. This limits interpretation because post-exposure results may not reflect in-service behavior accurately.

The evidence also highlights that experimental methods can differ substantially. For example, one study used steady-state tests, another used transient-state tests, and another used cyclic thermal exposure [N1-F1][N6-R3]. This introduces variability in the observed properties because dwell time, temperature rate, and thermal cycling can alter the measured response [N1-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence therefore supports the conclusion that temperature-dependent CFRP data are best interpreted as context-dependent, with model choice and experimental protocol strongly influencing the observed trend [N3-F3][N1-F1].

## Integrated final answer on how longitudinal tensile strength and modulus change across temperature regimes relative to Tg

The longitudinal tensile strength and modulus of unidirectional carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites change in a predictable but context-dependent way as temperature varies below, near, and above the glass transition temperature (Tg). The overall pattern is: **modulus tends to decrease with increasing temperature**, while **strength generally declines as well**, with the sharpest changes occurring near and above Tg. The exact shape of the curve depends on temperature history, dwell time, matrix softening, fiber-matrix interaction, and the measurement protocol used [N2-R3][N2-R2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

---

## Below Tg: gradual but measurable decline in strength and modulus

Below Tg, CFRP behavior is still dominated by the glassy matrix, which remains relatively stiff and load-bearing. As temperature increases toward Tg from below, the matrix stiffens less and becomes more thermally sensitive, which weakens the overall stiffness of the composite. The evidence indicates that matrix softening reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. This means that the composite’s stiffness is not only governed by the fiber but also by the matrix and their interaction.

Regarding strength, the evidence suggests that strength can decrease with increasing temperature even below Tg. A study on CFRP plates exposed to elevated temperatures reported that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3]. Another study on CFRP tendons reported that strength dropped dramatically when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C, although this is near- or above-Tg behavior rather than strictly below-Tg [N2-R2]. The review evidence also states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, whereas lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that, below Tg, strength may decrease gradually, though the rate depends on matrix softening and interfacial degradation.

The longitudinal tensile strength and modulus of unidirectional carbon fiber-reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites change in a predictable but context-dependent way as temperature varies below, near, and above the glass transition temperature (Tg). The overall pattern is: **modulus tends to decrease with increasing temperature**, while **strength generally declines as well**, with the sharpest changes occurring near and above Tg. The exact shape of the curve depends on temperature history, dwell time, matrix softening, fiber-matrix interaction, and the measurement protocol used [N2-R3][N2-R2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

---

## Below Tg: gradual but measurable decline in strength and modulus

Below Tg, CFRP behavior is still dominated by the glassy matrix, which remains relatively stiff and load-bearing. As temperature increases toward Tg from below, the matrix stiffens less and becomes more thermally sensitive, which weakens the overall stiffness of the composite. The evidence indicates that matrix softening reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. This means that the composite’s stiffness is not only governed by the fiber but also by the matrix and their interaction.

Regarding strength, the evidence suggests that strength can decrease with increasing temperature even below Tg. A study on CFRP plates exposed to elevated temperatures reported that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3]. Another study on CFRP tendons reported that strength dropped dramatically when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C, although this is near- or above-Tg behavior rather than strictly below-Tg [N2-R2]. The review evidence also states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, whereas lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This supports the idea that, below Tg, strength may decrease gradually, though the rate depends on matrix softening and interfacial degradation.

The role of matrix plasticization and fiber-matrix interaction is central. The evidence explicitly notes that matrix softening near or above Tg reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. It also emphasizes that compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach Tg, which is consistent with the idea that fiber-matrix interaction weakens as the matrix becomes more thermally active [N4-F4]. Fiber breakage, on the other hand, is described as significantly influencing the loss of stiffness in the laminate, but not its strength [N4-R1]. This suggests that below Tg, stiffness loss is more strongly tied to matrix and interfacial degradation than to fiber fracture, while strength may decline more slowly or less visibly.

Overall, below Tg, the evidence is consistent with a **gradual decrease in both strength and modulus as temperature increases**, but the exact trend is not uniform. Some studies suggest a gradual decrease in strength and modulus with increasing temperature [N2-R3], while others indicate that modulus may be relatively stable or only slowly affected below Tg [N3-R4]. The clearest pattern is that matrix softening and fiber-matrix interaction govern the temperature-dependent response, with strength more sensitive to interfacial degradation than to fiber failure [N4-R1][N4-F4].

---

## Near Tg: mixed transition effects on strength and modulus

Near Tg, the transition effects are marked by a **sharp or mixed response**, depending on the direction of approach and the measurement protocol. The evidence indicates that the transition is not a simple continuous or abrupt change; it is influenced by temperature history, dwell time, and the state of the polymer matrix [N4-F4][N5-F4].

Modulus and strength change differently near Tg. Some studies report that the strength of CFRP strip and rod dropped dramatically when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C [N2-R2]. This suggests an abrupt drop in strength as temperature crosses Tg. In contrast, another study on CFRP plates exposed to elevated temperatures found that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3]. This implies that modulus may remain relatively stable or change only slightly near Tg, while strength declines more prominently. The review evidence also states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, whereas lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This supports the interpretation that near Tg, the material moves from a stiffer, more brittle state to a softer, more ductile state.

The transition is also strongly affected by temperature rate and dwell time. The evidence notes that compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach Tg, and that the rate of quasi-isotropic laminate’s tensile softening and onset of failure under low applied tensile stresses is influenced by the ply stacking pattern [N4-F4]. Another study on CFRP plates under elevated temperatures found that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while the elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3], which suggests that dwell time and temperature history can smooth the apparent transition. The review also states that tensile strength and elasticity modulus do not deteriorate linearly with temperature, and that experimental results do not always align with linear extrapolation [N3-F3]. This implies that the transition near Tg can appear continuous in some studies and more abrupt in others, depending on the measurement protocol.

In summary, near Tg, the transition effects are **mixed**: modulus may remain relatively stable or change only slightly, while strength often decreases sharply as temperature crosses Tg [N2-R2][N2-R3]. The transition is not cleanly continuous or abrupt; it is influenced by matrix softening, fiber-matrix interaction, temperature history, and dwell time [N4-F4][N5-F4]. The evidence supports the interpretation that near Tg the material moves from a stiffer, more brittle state to a softer, more ductile state, with strength declining more prominently than modulus in some cases [N3-F3][N5-F4].

---

## Above Tg: strong decrease in modulus and progressive loss of strength

Above Tg, the mechanical response of CFRP becomes dominated by matrix softening, viscoelasticity, and long-term damage accumulation. The evidence is consistent that modulus decreases with increasing temperature above Tg, and in some cases, the decrease is dramatic. A review explicitly states that elevated temperatures reduce modulus and strength, while lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. Another study on CFRP plates found that tensile strength and elongation decrease gradually with increasing temperature, while elastic modulus shows negligible change [N2-R3], but this is not strong evidence for above-Tg behavior alone. A broader review on temperature-dependent CFRP mechanical properties states that studies have shown CFRP composites to decrease in tensile properties with increasing temperature, with the tensile properties mainly dependent on factors such as temperature and mechanical factors [N3-R2]. This supports the general conclusion that modulus and strength decline above Tg.

The strength response above Tg is more complex. Some studies report a significant drop in tensile strength with increasing temperature, including a 68% reduction in tensile strength after high-temperature exposure [N3-R5]. Another study found that CFRP tendons showed a dramatic drop in strength when temperature reached and exceeded Tg around 80°C and Td around 300°C [N2-R2]. The review evidence also notes that tensile properties decrease with increasing temperature and that the transition from brittle to ductile behavior occurs above Tg, with modulus and strength dropping [N3-F3]. These findings indicate that strength decreases above Tg, but the exact rate and magnitude depend on temperature, exposure time, and matrix degradation.

A key mechanism above Tg is matrix softening, which weakens the composite and increases damage accumulation. The evidence states that matrix softening near or above Tg reduces load transfer efficiency and increases fiber buckling failure on the compressive side [N4-F4]. It also notes that compression, in-plane shear, and interlaminar shear strengths drop by over 50% as temperatures approach Tg, which is consistent with a broader temperature-dependent degradation trend [N4-F4]. Above Tg, this softening becomes more pronounced, and the matrix is no longer able to support as much load, so strength declines more sharply.

Viscoelasticity and long-term creep/damage accumulation are important above Tg. The review explicitly states that elevated temperatures induce a transition from brittle to ductile behavior, reducing modulus and strength, while lower temperatures enhance tensile strength but decrease toughness [N3-F3]. This implies that above Tg, the material behaves more viscoelastically, and the response is not purely elastic. The review also emphasizes that geometric parameters and joint configurations can significantly influence failure mechanisms and mechanical behavior, suggesting that above-Tg damage is not only a matter of material properties but also of stress concentrations and long-term loading history [N3-F3]. The evidence does not provide a detailed viscoelastic model for CFRP in this wave, but it does support the interpretation that long-term exposure above Tg leads to cumulative damage and a progressive loss of strength.

In summary, above Tg, modulus decreases with increasing temperature, and strength generally decreases as well, often more sharply. The main drivers are matrix softening, fiber-matrix interaction loss, and long-term damage accumulation. The evidence is strongest for a decrease in strength and modulus above Tg, with some studies showing dramatic reductions [N2-R2][N3-R5], but it is also clear that the exact temperature dependence can vary depending on exposure conditions and material composition [N3-F3].
